chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said from Ibn Sinan from Ibn Muskan from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The length of the saddle of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was one cubit, and when he prayed, he placed it in front of him to shield himself from those who would pass in front of him.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: These narrations are understood as indicating preference (mustahabb), not that if one does not do it, their prayer is invalid, and that which indicates this is what has been narrated:

key_terms.اِسْتِحْبَاب: Recommendation or preferred status in Islamic law
key_terms.ذِرَاع: Cubit, a unit of length measurement
key_terms.رَحْل: Saddle or small stool used as a screen during prayer

ai.seo_question: Is using a screen (sutrah) during prayer obligatory or recommended in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the Prophet’s use of his saddle as a *sutrah* (prayer screen), noting its length of one cubit to shield the prayer space from passersby. Shaykh al-Tusi’s compiler, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, clarifies that this practice is *mustahabb* (recommended) rather than *wajib* (obligatory), ensuring that the validity of the prayer is not compromised if one prays without a screen. This distinction highlights the Shia juristic approach to distinguishing between prophetic customs and binding legal requirements in ritual purity and prayer mechanics.
